title: Pain de Campagne (Rustic Sourdough Boule)
summary: A slow-risen country sourdough boule with a touch of wholemeal, baked in a hot covered pot for a dark, crackling crust and an open, glossy crumb.
equipment: 23 cm round banneton or bowl lined with a floured cloth
razor blade or very sharp knife

ingredients.note: room temperature, plus 20 ml held back

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt

steps.title: Build the levain
steps.text: The evening before, stir the active starter with the 40 g bread flour, 10 g wholemeal flour and 50 ml water at about 26 °C until smooth. Cover and leave 8-12 hours at room temperature, until doubled and bubbly on top. A ripe levain gives the dough plenty of lift and a rounded, mild sourness.

steps.title: Mix and rest
steps.text: Stir the 450 g bread flour and 100 g wholemeal flour with 370 ml water, keeping back 20 ml, into a rough, shaggy dough. Cover and leave 30 minutes. This rest lets the flour drink up the water and start forming gluten on its own, so less work is needed later.

steps.title: Add salt and levain
steps.text: Scatter the salt over the dough, add the levain and the held-back water, then squeeze and fold everything together by hand until no dry streaks or pockets of levain remain. Adding the salt after the rest keeps it from tightening the dough too early.

steps.title: Bulk rise with folds
steps.text: Cover and leave for 4-5 hours at about 24-26 °C, giving 4 sets of stretch-and-folds during the first 2 hours, 30 minutes apart. The dough is ready when it has grown by about half, looks domed and shows bubbles at the edges. Folding builds strength gently, which is what supports an open, irregular crumb.

steps.title: Shape the boule
steps.text: Tip the dough out, pre-shape it into a loose round and rest it 20 minutes. Then shape firmly into a tight boule, building tension across the surface, and place it seam-up in the banneton dusted with rice flour. Rice flour has no gluten, so it does not stick to the damp dough.

steps.title: Cold retard
steps.text: Cover and refrigerate for 12-16 hours. The long chill deepens the flavour and firms the dough, making it far easier to score cleanly.

steps.title: Preheat the pot
steps.text: Put the lidded cast-iron pot in the oven and heat to 250 °C (230 °C fan) for 45 minutes. A thoroughly hot pot delivers a burst of heat to the base and traps the loaf's own steam for a big rise.

steps.title: Score and bake
steps.text: Turn the cold loaf onto baking paper, slash the top about 1 cm deep and lower it into the pot with the paper. Bake covered for 20 minutes, then uncover, lower the oven to 230 °C (210 °C fan) and bake 20-25 minutes more, until very dark brown all over and the centre reads about 96 °C. The loaf should sound hollow when tapped underneath.

steps.title: Cool fully
steps.text: Lift the loaf onto a wire rack and cool for at least 2 hours before cutting. The crumb is still setting as it cools, so slicing early leaves it gummy.

tips: Use the float test or simply look for a domed, bubbly, doubled levain; an under-ripe levain is the most common cause of a dense loaf.
Do not under-bake: a pale crust tastes flat, so push the colour to a deep brown.
If your kitchen is cool, the bulk rise will take longer; judge by the dough's volume and bubbles, not just the clock.
Use oven gloves and take great care lowering the loaf into the very hot pot; the paper sling keeps your hands clear.
storage: Keep the cooled loaf wrapped in a cloth or paper bag at room temperature for up to 3 days, cut side down on the board. Slice and freeze for up to 1 month, toasting from frozen. Cool leftovers in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours (within 1 hour on a day above 32°C).
